transcript.content: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?

Hello. Well, I... I guess I'm here because I just keep messing up these little things. It's, well, it's really getting under my skin, to be honest. I mean, I'm 62, I've got plenty of time on my hands now that I'm not working, so you'd think I'd be able to just slow down and pay attention to what I'm doing, but... well, for instance, just last week down at the senior center. They have these classes, you see, and I was looking at the schedule for one—it was a local history thing, I've always liked history—anyway, I looked right at the class sheet, right at the paper, and I somehow managed to write down the completely wrong time. Just completely messed it up and showed up when the room was already locked up and empty. 

And it's not just that, it's stuff around the house, too. Like I was out in the garage a couple days ago working on a little project. I took my tape measure, measured this board once—which I know better than to do, you know the old saying, measure twice, cut once, my father used to drill that into my head—but I just kind of glanced at it, skipped right over the small print, those little fraction marks on the tape, and just made the cut. And of course, wouldn't you know it, it was a hair short. The whole piece of wood, just useless. It’s just... it’s always these tiny little details that I just gloss over, and it's happening all the time lately. I just don't know why I can't seem to get the small stuff right.
Looking back to when you were in school as a child or teenager, did you have similar trouble paying attention to details or making careless mistakes?

Oh, school... well, now that you mention it, yes. Very much so. It's funny you ask about that because I was actually just going through some old boxes in the attic a few months back—my wife has been on me to clear out some space, you know how that goes, collecting dust and taking up room—and I found a stack of my old report cards from elementary school. My mother had saved them all in this little green cardboard folder, bless her heart. 

And looking at them, it was like reading a broken record. I mean, going all the way back to, gosh, second or third grade, I had this teacher, Mrs. Higgins, and she wrote—and practically all the other teachers after her wrote the exact same thing—she wrote that I was a bright boy, very capable, but I just could not keep track of my things or stay focused. I was always forgetting my textbooks at school when I needed them for the evening's assignments, or I'd actually sit down and do the homework at the kitchen table, and then just completely lose the paper somewhere between my front door and the classroom. It used to drive my mother absolutely up the wall. 

And the comments on those report cards, they always said I was just staring out the window, daydreaming, watching the clouds or the custodian mowing the lawn, and I wouldn't get a lick of work done unless Mrs. Higgins or someone was standing right over my shoulder, tapping my desk to keep me on track. So, I suppose, yes, this isn't exactly a new problem, even if it feels a lot more frustrating now with the woodworking and the schedules. I just always figured it was a kid thing, you know? You just assume you'll outgrow staring out the window and forgetting your papers by the time you're a grown man, let alone sixty-two.
